title: Schnabel argues that a common European corporate regime could help promising firms grow across borders
summary: Isabel Schnabel argues that Europe can raise productivity by giving companies an easier way to build businesses across the Single Market. Her proposal is an optional European corporate form available to companies of any size or sector. She starts by separating several issues often grouped together as Europe's growth problem: differences in working hours and income distribution, genuine weakness in productivity per hour, and barriers that keep successful businesses from expanding. The speech and accompanying slides present evidence about these distinctions. They make an economic case for a legal proposal without putting a forecast value on its future benefits.

Slide 6 illustrates what international income comparisons leave out. A US employee works about 40 more days a year than the average euro area employee. If euro area workers supplied US hours at unchanged hourly productivity and employment rates, real GDP per person would be 21% higher, closing around two thirds of the measured gap. That calculation changes one input while holding others fixed. It says nothing about what hours workers would choose or how productivity would respond. The richest tenth receives about 37% of after-tax national income in the United States versus roughly 27% in the euro area. US technology-sector gains have also been concentrated. Slide 9 nevertheless shows a genuine euro area shortfall in growth of hourly output and capital deepening.

The comparison within the currency union matters as much as the comparison across the Atlantic. Spain, Portugal and Greece have strengthened investment or employment since their crises, while the potential growth figures on slide 12 are projections. Schnabel cites renewable electricity in Spain and common EU investment resources as examples of how policy can support a recovery. Germany's real GDP per capita, by contrast, fell 0.5% between 2019 and 2024. Its earlier years of large trade surpluses produced average annual GDP growth of only 1.4% from 1999 to 2019. Real private consumption has grown by less than 1% per year on average since 1999. Mobile German companies could invest abroad even while domestic capital spending was weak. Whether public investment can draw their capital back depends, in her account, on project quality and structural reform.

Schnabel locates a wider European problem between invention and commercial scale. A business seeking customers and capital across borders has to deal with multiple corporate regimes, registries and procedures. Growth-stage funding and an attractive exit through a liquid public market can be harder to find than seed funding. Firms with more than 250 employees account for almost 60% of US employment but nearer 20% in many euro area countries. Slide 18 reports estimates of internal trade barriers equivalent to tariffs of 96% for services and 67% for goods. These are estimated equivalents of many impediments. They are neither actual tariff bills nor a measure of the saving that one company-law change would deliver.

Under the proposed regime, a company could incorporate digitally using common rules on governance, shareholder rights and employee financial compensation. Schnabel supports a directly applicable EU regulation so that national transposition does not recreate legal fragmentation. National labour law, social security and taxation would remain national, and businesses could continue to use domestic corporate forms. She also identifies watered-down insolvency provisions as a risk. The proposed mechanism is that greater legal predictability could make cross-border growth and funding easier and keep more of the value created by European founders in Europe. Its investment implications depend on which obstacles the eventual text removes and whether funding and exit markets develop alongside it.

questions.question: Would the proposed European company form change where growth-stage firms raise capital and keep operations?
questions.detail: Track firms eligible to opt in against comparable national incorporations, recording later fundraising, cross-border sales, employment and headquarters moves. Company registries, filings and funding disclosures would distinguish a cheaper incorporation process from a genuine change in where firms scale. The latter matters more for the investable European growth-company universe.

questions.question: Which barriers in the services estimate are actually addressed by the proposed law?
questions.detail: Map the proposed rules on shareholder rights, governance and insolvency against the frictions faced by businesses entering a second EU market. Compare sectors with large estimated trade barriers but different licensing, labour and tax requirements. Legal texts and company disclosures could indicate whether the 96% tariff-equivalent estimate is relevant for particular businesses or mainly reflects barriers outside the proposal.

questions.question: Will German public investment attract private capital to Germany?
questions.detail: Compare project execution, domestic fixed investment and companies' outward investment with their earlier trends. Separate public procurement winners from companies whose returns depend on better infrastructure or energy supply. The fiscal measures could support near-term revenues without reversing investment-location decisions. Budget execution, the capital accounts and geographic company investment disclosures would help distinguish the two horizons.
